1.title: Product Backlog, Product Goal and Refinement
1.text: Welcome to Module 10: Product Backlog, Product Goal and Refinement. This starts the artifacts block. You will learn what the Product Backlog is, why it is never finished, how items become ready for a Sprint through refinement, and what the Product Goal does. You will also see how the three commitments fit together.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose and attributes of the Product Backlog. Explain why it is emergent. Name three attributes of a Product Backlog item. Describe refinement, with three activities and two reasons. Explain the Product Goal and the three commitments. And spot the traps: a complete backlog, refinement as an event, and required formats.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Backlog of 140 Items
1.text: At RideLoop, the Product Backlog holds about one hundred and forty items, and only the top twelve are refined. Grace Whitfield wants every item fully detailed and sized right now. Meanwhile, the Station Crew's item, to report a broken bike with a photo, sits at position sixty, and they are frustrated. As Scrum Master, you ask what a healthy Product Backlog looks like. This module gives you the answer.

1.title: Artifacts and Commitments
1.text: First, the big picture. Scrum's artifacts represent work or value, and they are built for transparency, so that everyone who inspects them starts from the same facts. Each artifact holds one commitment. The Product Backlog holds the Product Goal. The Sprint Backlog holds the Sprint Goal. The Increment holds the Definition of Done. Three artifacts, three commitments, always in those pairs. A common trap swaps them.

1.title: The Product Backlog
1.text: The Guide defines the Product Backlog as "an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product." It is the single source of work for the Scrum Team. The Product Owner is accountable for it, though the work may be delegated. And what is not in the Product Backlog is not what the team undertakes. At RideLoop, that means a healthy Product Backlog is not fully detailed up front: only the top twelve of about one hundred and forty items are refined. Maya orders the rest, and the Station Crew convinces Maya; they do not push their item up themselves. For the exam, remember two words: emergent, and ordered.

1.title: Attributes of the Product Backlog
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three attributes. Emergent: it changes as the product and the understanding change. Ordered: in a sequence set by the Product Owner. The single source of work. Owned by one person, the Product Owner. Transparent: visible and understood by everyone. It holds the Product Goal, with the rest emerging to fulfill it. And refined continuously, with items detailed as needed. Pick any three that you can explain.

1.title: Why It Is Emergent
1.text: Why is the Product Backlog emergent? These reasons go beyond the Guide, but they follow from its theory. The work is complex, so the full need is unknown at the start. Every Sprint Review brings feedback and changes in the environment. Learning during the Sprints reveals new, changed or unneeded items. And items are detailed only when needed, so effort is not wasted. The earlier edition said never complete, living, and requirements; the current wording is emergent and work.

1.title: Product Backlog Items
1.text: What attributes does an item have? The Guide names three: a description, so that everyone understands the item; its order in the Product Backlog; and its size, which the Developers decide. It adds that the attributes depend on the domain of the work. Many teams also add value, which helps ordering, and test or acceptance notes, which show when the item is complete; those two go beyond the Guide. In the earlier edition you will find the word estimate. User stories and story points are not in the Guide at all.

1.title: Ready for Selection, and Who Sizes
1.text: When is an item ready for Sprint Planning? When the Scrum Team can get it Done within one Sprint. Items usually reach that state through refinement. Who sizes them? The Developers, because they will do the work. The Product Owner may help them understand and select trade-offs, for example by simplifying an item, but does not set the size. Large or vague items are refined first.

1.title: Product Backlog Refinement
1.text: Refinement means breaking down and further defining items into smaller, more precise ones. It is an ongoing activity. The Product Backlog is refined whenever needed during the Sprint, and the Scrum Team may refine items in Sprint Planning too. Refinement is not one of the five events. The Guide sets no required time, length or format. The Product Owner and the Developers collaborate on it.

1.title: Refinement Activities
1.text: The learning objective asks for three refinement activities. They go beyond the Guide. Split large items into smaller ones, which is the Guide's own idea of breaking down. Add detail, such as a description and often the value. Size the items, which is for the Developers. Order or reorder them, which is for the Product Owner. Clarify with stakeholders and users: questions, examples, constraints and dependencies. And remove or update items that are stale, which keeps the Product Backlog useful. Name any three.

1.title: Reasons for Refinement
1.text: And at least two reasons for refinement. These also go beyond the Guide. Shared understanding: everyone knows why an item matters and what it needs. Ready items for Planning, which makes Planning faster and more reliable. Better forecasts, because smaller, clearer items build confidence. Transparency: the Product Backlog is visible and understood. Early discovery of risks and dependencies, before the Sprint. And adaptation, because new information changes the order of the work.

1.title: The Product Goal
1.text: The Product Goal describes "a future state of the product" that serves as a target for the team to plan against. It is the team's long-term objective, and it lives in the Product Backlog. The Product Owner develops and communicates it. The team works on one Product Goal at a time: it must fulfill or abandon one before taking on the next. A product has a clear boundary, known stakeholders and defined users, and exists to deliver value.

1.title: The Three Artifacts Compared
1.text: Compare the three artifacts. The Product Backlog is the single source of work, its commitment is the Product Goal, and the Product Owner is accountable for it. The Sprint Backlog is the Developers' plan for the Sprint, with the Sprint Goal, and lives for one Sprint. The Increment is a usable step toward the Product Goal, with the Definition of Done, and the whole Scrum Team is accountable for it.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. The Product Backlog is emergent and ordered, never complete up front. It is the single source of work: the Product Owner orders it, and stakeholders convince. The Developers size, and the Product Owner helps with trade-offs. Refinement is an ongoing activity with no prescribed time. Ready means it can be Done within one Sprint. One Product Goal at a time. And user stories and story points are not required. Estimate and the ten percent guideline are old wording, and grooming is an older name for refinement.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Product Backlog is emergent, ordered, and the single source of work. Items have a description, an order and a size, and the Developers size them. An item is ready when it can be Done within one Sprint. Refinement is ongoing: split, detail, size, order and clarify. The Product Goal is one future state at a time. And the commitments are Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The RideLoop Developers do all refinement in one session on the day before each Sprint and never during the Sprint. What does the Guide say? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Product Backlog is refined whenever needed, including during the Sprint, and the team may also refine items in Sprint Planning. The Guide neither prescribes a refinement session nor limits when it happens.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A contractor tells Maya that Scrum requires every Product Backlog item to be a user story sized in story points. What is the right answer? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Guide names description, order and size, and says the attributes vary with the domain. It mentions neither user stories nor story points.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. In the middle of Sprint nine, a new city regulation creates an urgent item for RideLoop. What is the correct way to handle it? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Product Owner orders it in the Product Backlog and negotiates with the Developers whether it enters the Sprint, without endangering the Sprint Goal. Cancelling is only for an obsolete Sprint Goal.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which pairing of artifacts and commitments is correct? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Product Backlog holds the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog holds the Sprint Goal, and the Increment holds the Definition of Done. The other options each swap at least one pair.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. When is a Product Backlog item deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. When the Scrum Team can get the item Done within one Sprint. Items usually reach that point through refinement. Written approval, story points and position alone do not make an item ready.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: A. Refinement is ongoing. Question two: D. The Guide requires neither user stories nor story points. Question three: A. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog and negotiates scope. Question four: D. Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done. Question five: C. Ready means it can be Done within one Sprint. That completes Module 10. Next, Module 11 covers the Sprint Backlog and the Sprint Goal.
